title: Finding Exoplanets
sub: we find them by watching a star get very slightly dimmer
summary: A planet crossing its star blocks a disc of it and the brightness drops by the ratio of the areas. Change the planet, the orbit and the star, and watch the dip move against what our instruments can actually detect.

sources.claim: Transit method and the first measured transit
sources.cite: Charbonneau, Brown, Latham & Mayor 2000, ApJ 529, L45

sources.claim: Depth = (R_p/R_star)^2, limb darkening u ~ 0.6 in the visible
Kepler photometric precision ~20 ppm for bright quiet stars
JWST transit precision ~10 ppm per transit
Kepler's third law P^2 = a^3 / M_star
Equilibrium temperature with albedo 0.3 gives 255 K for Earth
sources.cite: standard result; the remaining 33 K is the greenhouse effect

open: The planet in the 3D view is drawn far larger than scale. At true scale an Earth against the Sun is under one pixel; the depth readout carries the honest number and the picture is a diagram.
Orbit radius is compressed logarithmically so a 0.05 AU and a 5 AU orbit can share one scene.
Limb darkening uses a single linear coefficient. Real fits use quadratic or non-linear laws and the coefficient depends on wavelength and stellar type.
Orbits are treated as circular. Eccentricity changes transit duration and the probability of transiting at all.
The instrument floors are order-of-magnitude figures for a bright, quiet star. Real detectability also depends on stellar variability, observing cadence and how many transits you can stack.
A transit gives radius only. Mass needs radial velocity, and without mass you cannot distinguish a rocky planet from a low-density one.
The habitable zone shown is the conservative one and assumes an Earth-like atmosphere. It is a rough guide to where liquid water could be stable, not a statement about habitability.
